articles.title: ‘I’m bringing together women who nourish me’: French film-maker Alice Diop on her debut installation
articles.summary: The Saint Omer director has gathered work by artists, writers, composers and poets for Geste de Consolation, set in the 60m-long central hall of the Palais d’Iena in Paris. Alice Diop has just returned to France from California when we speak.
body: Diop had been attending a two-week celebration of her work organised by the French department at University of California, Berkeley, in which academics pored over her documentaries ( Nous (We), Vers La Tendresse (Towards Tenderness)) and her first feature film, Saint Omer, which received the Silver Lion in Venice in 2022. The courtroom drama was inspired by a real trial that Diop attended, of a Senegalese woman who had allowed her baby to drown in the sea. Over two hours, it explored the complexities of race, culture and motherhood in contemporary France. The film was the first by a black female director to be entered by France as its official entry in the 2023 Academy Awards.

“To be studied like that, in such a temple of intellectual resistance, I was bowled over,” says Diop of UC Berkeley. “As a film-maker, it’s not up to me to analyse my work. But listening to them, it was good to feel understood.”

articles.title: Tom Cruise Said He Doesn’t Make Movies for ‘Opening Weekend’ Right Before ‘Digger’ Bombed: ‘You Hope to Make a Film That Can Last’
articles.summary: Tom Cruise suffered one of his worst box office openings in history with “Digger,” Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s satirical black comedy that bombed with $8 million in North America on a production budget north of $160 million. But Cruise isn’t one to judge a movie based on its first weekend in theaters.
body: “They transcend… you just hope you can make a film that can last,” Cruise said. “So many things happen when you open a movie. I was fortunate to release movies in the 80s and 90s, when movies would stay in the theater for a year. With ‘Rain Man’ and ‘Born on the Fourth of July,’ these movie would just play and play for a year. How can I make a film that can translate and last and evolve? And I feel that way…. that is ‘Digger,’ it’s one of those movies.”

With its production budget between $160 million and $180 million, plus a $100 million marketing budget, “Digger” would need to gross $350 million in theaters worldwide just to break even at the box office. That figure will be impossible to hit after the movie’s $20 million global start. The movie is now primed to lose at least $150 million to $200 million theatrically.

articles.title: ‘Star Trek: The Next Generation’ Star Gates McFadden to Write Dr. Crusher Comic Book Series (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Gates McFadden is returning to the iconic character Dr. Beverly Crusher. Variety has learned exclusively that McFadden is penning the limited comic series “Star Trek: Crusher” with IDW Publishing.
body: The announcement of the comic book comes as the “Star Trek” franchise is celebrating its 60th anniversary, with the original series having premiered on Sept. 8, 1966. Paramount has already held a number of events in celebration of the milestone, including screenings of fan-favorite episodes, television specials, and more.

“IDW’s bold celebration of ‘Star Trek’s’ 60th anniversary was just the beginning of our stellar plans for the iconic franchise,” stated Davidi Jonas, IDW CEO. “We are so fortunate to have Gates McFadden beam into the world of comics and reprise her role of Beverly Crusher, but this time as the writer. There is a 20 year gap in the fan-favorite character’s story. Who better to tell it than Beverly Crusher herself?”

IDW has also recently released the anthology “Star Trek: 60th Anniversary Special” and “Star Trek” #1. Up next, the company will publish “Star Trek: Zero Point,” which features commander Raffi Musiker, beginning Oct. 14.

articles.title: Indian Streamer JioHotstar Enters Middle East and North Africa Through Starzplay Partnership
articles.summary: India’s largest streamer, JioHotstar, has moved into the Middle East and North Africa, teaming with Abu Dhabi-based Starzplay to reach a region the company considers key for South Asian viewers. The MENA launch comes after earlier rollouts in the U.K., Canada and Singapore.
body: Hindi, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu and Bangla-language titles are all part of the mix. The Malayalam catalog is especially deep, reflecting the weight of the region’s audience hailing from Kerala, where it is the dominant language.

Starzplay CEO Maaz Sheikh said that the region’s streamers will grow by pairing strong brands and giving viewers more for their money. “Audiences should not have to navigate an increasingly fragmented market to find the entertainment that matters to them. Bringing JioHotstar to Starzplay is a strategic investment in that future, combining the strength of India’s storytelling with our understanding of this region and the audiences we serve,” he said.

JioHotstar content is included in Starzplay’s Plus plan, which costs AED34.99 ($9.50) a month. The Max plan, at AED49.99 ($13.60) a month, pairs the full JioHotstar lineup with Starzplay’s sports rights, cricket among them. Starzplay positions itself as the region’s main destination for cricket.

articles.title: Axe used by Jack Nicholson in The Shining for sale as part of Stanley Kubrick auction
articles.summary: Exclusive: Weapon is one of hundreds of items to be sold as part of the influential late director’s personal archive. A special effects axe wielded by Jack Nicholson as he delivered his chillingly manic line “Here’s Johnny!” in the 1980 horror movie The Shining is to go on sale.
body: Nicholson’s character, Jack Torrance, uses an axe to hack out an opening in a locked door protecting his terrified wife Wendy, played by Shelley Duvall. It is also the murder weapon in the killing of Scatman Crothers’ character, Dick Hallorann. One of cinema’s most famous axes could be yours for a list price of between £30,000 and £50,000.
It is one of hundreds of items in the first auction of the personal archive of The Shining’s influential director, Stanley Kubrick, who died in 1999.

The sale includes several other lots from the film, including two sky-blue dresses worn by the twin sisters Alexa and Alexie Grady. They appear in the frocks in a memorable scene when they invite Torrance’s son, Danny, to “come play with us” as he pedals on his tricycle through the corridors of the Overlook Hotel.

The boy’s trike is not part of the sale, but a clapperboard used in the film is one of four from Kubrick’s movies to go under the hammer. The others are are from 2001: A Space Odyssey, the 1975 historical drama Barry Lyndon and Kubrick’s last film, Eyes Wide Shut.

articles.title: ‘We got that bad guy and took him down!’ Jaclyn Smith on the fun, friendship and frustration of Charlie’s Angels
articles.summary: It’s 50 years since Smith joined TV’s bikini-clad crime fighters alongside Farrah Fawcett and Kate Jackson. She talks about the love she found on set, the harassment she endured off it and the drug-taking she did her best to ignore.
body: For a TV show that only ran for five years, Charlie’s Angels packs a punch like a bikini-wearing big-hair-flicking private investigator. “We never thought we’d be talking about it 50 years later,” says Jaclyn Smith, the only original Angel to make it to the end of the show’s run. Smith, 80, has now written a memoir, I Once Knew a Guy Called Charlie – she is not, you gather, the type of actor to want to distance herself from her defining project.

As I read her book, and speak to her over Zoom, she comes across as sensible, hardworking and optimistic. Also lucky: loving and supportive parents, agents who seem to appear from nowhere and offer her work, an early hit show, a gift for making friends and getting over heartbreak. Even when she was diagnosed with breast cancer more than 20 years ago, terrifying as it was, it was caught early and successfully treated. Her positive outlook seems to extend to the excesses of US TV in the 1970s and 80s (drug use on set only gets a brief mention); her three ex-husbands get off fairly lightly; and any difficulties – her OCD, the men who stalked her at the height of her fame – are not dwelled on.

articles.title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
articles.summary: The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition.
body: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape.

The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers.
It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.
The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network.

articles.title: Celibidache was a musical visionary, an uncompromising perfectionist – and my father
articles.summary: The legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings. His son, writer of a new film about him, remembers a loving yet intransigent and demanding father.
body: M y father, Sergiu Celibidache, loved children more than anything because they are free and true to themselves. And yet, he once made a young boy wet himself when he dared to ask for an autograph, shouting at the poor child as if he had committed a federal crime because he knew there was a black market selling his signature behind his back.

I grew up a privileged child with presents from all around the world. I was spoiled – to the despair of my mother, who always tried to keep my feet on the ground. But the gifts were part of my father’s way of making up for his long absences – he was often away touring with his orchestras.

As a young boy I had very little understanding that my father was a world-renowned conductor. I always missed him terribly when he was away, and yet he was nonetheless always very present in my life, and we were close. He was generous and attentive. There were frequent speeches about the less privileged and our duty to do something for them, and he was always eager to share stories of his picturesque childhood in Iași, Romania and his many adventures after leaving home to pursue music, without any support from his family.
points: The legendary conductor was acclaimed for his dazzling music-making, and infamous for his hatred of recordings.

I grew up a privileged child with presents from all around the world.

articles.title: Queen pays tribute to 'irrepressible' Jeffrey Archer
articles.summary: The bestselling author and former politician died on Monday at the age of 86.
body: Queen Camilla has paid tribute to the bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer, who has died at the age of 86.
"Seldom does an author get to live a life as rich, varied and colourful as any of the characters in their books, or with as many surprising plot twists," the Queen said in a statement.
She added that Archer was "not without flaw", but that "friends will recall him as an irrepressible life force through all the many differing chapters of his life".
The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star.
